name: G-Model & 930 Turbo
tagline: Impact bumpers, turbochargers and sixteen years
description:
Porsche began series production of the second-generation 911 in August 1973 for the 1974 model year. The rework added telescopic impact bumpers that met the US 5-mph crash rule, a full-width rear light band, a longer and more comfortable body (4,291 mm) and — for the first time across the range — the 2.7-litre flat-six that had previously been reserved for the Carrera RS 2.7. The launch landed in the middle of the 1973 oil crisis, yet the car became the best-selling 911 to that point.

Over sixteen years the range grew in two directions at once. The normally aspirated cars stepped from 2.7 to 3.0 litres in 1976, to the 180–204 PS 911 SC (1978–83) and finally to the 231 PS Carrera 3.2 (1984–89, with the G50 gearbox from 1987). At the top, the 930 Turbo arrived in 1975 with 260 PS, grew to 3.3 litres and 300 PS with the first production intercooler in 1978, and spawned the Sonderwunsch Flachbau slantnose, the 330 PS Werksleistungssteigerung kit, the 1989 Turbo S and the UK-only Turbo LE.

Bodywork widened too: Coupé and Targa throughout, a factory Cabriolet from 1982/83, and the 1989 Speedster that closed the generation. Porsche counts 198,496 G-Series cars built between 1973 and 1989 (a second Newsroom datasheet gives 196,397). Strictly, "G-Series" denotes only the 1974 model year — H, J, K and later programme codes followed — but the G-model name stuck.

variants.engine: 2,687 cc air-cooled flat-six (Type 911/92 for MY1974), Bosch K-Jetronic CIS
variants.transmission: 915 5-speed manual (4-speed manual for some MY1976 cars)
variants.description: The entry-level G-Model arrived with the 1974 model year, its 2.7-litre flat-six carried over from the Carrera RS 2.7 but fed by Bosch K-Jetronic rather than mechanical injection. Federal impact bumpers and the full-width rear light band defined its looks, and Coupé and Targa were the only bodies offered. Output was 150 PS (110 kW) through 1975 and rose to 165 PS (121 kW) for 1976–77, lifting top speed from 210 to 217 km/h. It was the volume car of the early range: roughly 17,000 Coupés and Targas left Zuffenhausen across four model years.

variants.name: 911 S 2.7

variants.description: The 911 S 2.7 sat in the middle of the early G-Model line-up: the same K-Jetronic 2.7-litre flat-six as the base car, but tuned to 175 PS (129 kW), a 25 PS gain over the entry model. Top speed rose to 225 km/h (140 mph) and 0–100 km/h fell to 7.6 seconds. Like every early G-Model it was offered as a Coupé or Targa, and it was produced alongside the rarer Kugelfischer-fed Carrera 2.7. Porsche dropped the S after 1977 as the range consolidated around 3.0-litre cars.

variants.name: 911 Carrera 2.7
variants.engine: 2,687 cc air-cooled flat-six, Bosch Kugelfischer mechanical injection
variants.description: For four years the Carrera 2.7 was the fastest normally aspirated 911 on the price list. Its 2,687 cc flat-six kept the Bosch Kugelfischer mechanical injection of the 1973 RS 2.7 and made 210 PS (154 kW), good for 0–100 km/h in 6.3 seconds and a 240 km/h (149 mph) top speed. A wider rear track gave the Carrera its Coke-bottle silhouette, and like the 2.7 S it was sold as a Coupé or Targa. European cars retained mechanical injection throughout; North America received K-Jetronic versions.

variants.description: The RS 3.0 was built in tiny numbers purely to homologate the 3.0-litre RSR racing car. Its 2,993 cc engine took the RSR's 95 mm bore and ran Kugelfischer mechanical injection on 9.8:1 compression, while the chassis gained wider Fuchs wheels, a reinforced suspension and 917-derived cross-drilled ventilated brakes. A systematic diet left the car around 900 kg dry. In road tune the six produced 230 PS (169 kW) at 6,200 rpm with 275 Nm at 5,000. Only 55–56 cars were completed in 1974.

variants.description: The RSR 3.0 was the pure competition car that the RS 3.0 existed to homologate. The Type 911/75 engine was bored to 2,996 cc and given twin-spark ignition, a dry sump and a six-piston Kugelfischer pump, revving to 8,000 rpm for 330 bhp (246 kW) and 314 Nm. Dry weight was about 900 kg, with 917-derived ventilated brakes and a reinforced 915 five-speed; top speed was 288 km/h (179 mph). The RSR became the most successful Group 4 racing car of its era, yet Porsche never published a 0–100 km/h time for it.

variants.name: 911 Turbo 3.0 (930)
variants.engine: 2,993 cc turbocharged flat-six (Type 930/50), K-Jetronic, 0.8 bar boost
variants.description: Unveiled at the Paris Motor Show in October 1974 and in showrooms from spring 1975, the 930 Turbo was the first turbocharged 911 and, at the time, the fastest production car sold in Germany. Its 2,993 cc flat-six ran 0.8 bar of boost for 260 PS (191 kW) and 343 Nm, pushing the wide-bodied Coupé to 250 km/h (155 mph) and 0–100 km/h in 5.4–5.5 seconds — all through a four-speed gearbox. The whale tail, flared arches and sudden boost earned it the "widowmaker" reputation. Porsche counts 2,819 cars to 1977; its own press material says 2,850.

variants.name: 911 Turbo 3.3 (930)
variants.power: 300 PS (221 kW) @5,500 rpm (330 PS with the WLS power kit)
variants.description: For 1978 the Turbo grew to 3,299 cc and gained an air-to-air intercooler tucked under a re-profiled "tea tray" wing — the first production car to use one. Output rose to 300 PS (221 kW) at 5,500 rpm with 412 Nm, yet top speed only edged up to 260 km/h (162 mph) while kerb weight passed 1,300 kg. A Werksleistungssteigerung kit lifted output to 330 PS. From February 1987 Targa and Cabriolet bodies joined the range, and for 1989 the four-speed was finally replaced by a five-speed Getrag G50. Roughly 18,770 were built (Porsche's own figure is 17,792).

variants.description: The Flachbau (slantnose) was Porsche's Sonderwunsch answer to customers who wanted their Turbo to look like a 935. Steel front wings dropped the headlights into the bumper — pop-up lamps from 1983 — while louvred rear-wheel air intakes and a deep front spoiler with an integral oil cooler completed the transformation. First customer cars left the Restoration Department in Werks 1 in 1982; production ran in three generations to 1989, when M505 (US) and M506 (rest-of-world) cars were finally built on the main line. Porsche counts 948 in total. With the 330 PS kit it was the fastest 930, at 275 km/h (171 mph).

Top speed rose to 270 km/h (168 mph). It also gained a five-speed G50 with limited-slip differential, a 7,000-rpm rev counter and a 300 km/h speedometer. Just 55 were built for 1989, 42 of them reserved for German customers.

variants.transmission: Getrag G50 5-speed manual with 40% limited-slip differential
variants.description: To close out fourteen years of 930 production, Porsche pulled 50 Coupés from the final G50 assembly batch and handed them to the Exclusive department at Zuffenhausen. Each LE got the 330 PS Sport Equipment engine — 30 PS above the standard Turbo — plus a limited-slip differential, rear-wheel air intakes, sill extensions and an Exclusive front spoiler with an integral oil cooler, evoking the 935. Inside there were heated electric sport seats, a three-spoke wheel with a gold crest and a numbered console plaque. One car was allocated to each UK Porsche Centre; 0–60 mph took 4.6 seconds.

variants.name: 911 Carrera 3.0
variants.engine: 2,994 cc air-cooled flat-six, Bosch K-Jetronic CIS
variants.description: The Carrera 3.0 replaced the 2.7 Carrera for 1976 and traded mechanical injection for K-Jetronic, costing it 7 kW: 147 kW (200 PS) at 6,000 rpm with 255 Nm. It was effectively the first road car with the bottom end that the 930 Turbo would use, and it became the mechanical template for the SC that followed. Performance stayed close to the 2.7 Carrera's — 0–100 km/h in about 6.3 seconds and a 230 km/h (143 mph) top speed — while the body remained narrow. Some 3,687 were built across 1976–77, roughly 30 per cent of them Targas.

variants.name: 911 SC
variants.engine: 2,994 cc air-cooled flat-six, Bosch K-Jetronic CIS
variants.description: Marketed as the last 911 — the 928 was meant to replace it — the SC arrived for 1978 with a 2,994 cc K-Jetronic flat-six and a heavier, galvanised body. Output climbed through its life: 180 PS (132 kW) for 1978–79, 188 PS (138 kW) for 1980 and 204 PS (150 kW) for 1981–83, with top speed rising from 220 to 235 km/h. It was also the first 911 with a factory Cabriolet — shown in Geneva in March 1982 and sold from the 1983 model year. Porsche built 60,265 SCs before the 3.2 Carrera replaced it.

variants.description: The SC RS was Porsche's stopgap Group B rally car, created while the 959 was still in development. Announced in June 1983 as the "911 SC RS – Gruppe B", it used the outgoing 3.0-litre SC platform because the new 3.2 would have pushed it into a heavier class. The Type 930/18 engine ran 10.3:1 compression on Kugelfischer injection for 250–255 bhp on the road and around 270 bhp in rally trim, with a 960 kg minimum weight. Twenty homologation cars were built — a 21st followed — and Prodrive ran six of them for the Rothmans Porsche Rally Team.

European cars made 231 PS (170 kW) at 5,900 rpm and 284 Nm, hitting 0–100 km/h in 6.1 seconds and 245 km/h (152 mph); North America got 207–217 hp engines on 9.5:1 compression. The 915 gearbox lasted to 1986 before the Getrag G50 with hydraulic clutch arrived for 1987. Coupé, Targa and Cabriolet were all offered, and 76,473 cars were built to 1989.

variants.description: The Club Sport was Porsche's "less is more" reply to the excess of the 1980s. Option M637 deleted the sunroof, rear seat, air conditioning, power windows, radio, sound insulation and underseal to save roughly 40–70 kg, while the engine gained hollow inlet valves, a revised intake and a raised 6,840 rpm rev limiter. Official output stayed at 231 PS, but kerb weight fell to about 1,160 kg, taking 0–60 mph to 5.1 seconds and top speed to 244 km/h (152 mph). Coupé-only, built from September 1987 to September 1989: 340 cars, 53 for the UK and 28 for the US.
